bodies.intuition: A dense model pushes every token through every parameter it owns. A mixture-of-experts model keeps many parallel sub-networks and wakes only a couple per token, chosen by a small router. The model can hold far more knowledge than it spends compute on, because you pay for the experts you wake up, not the ones you own.
bodies.engineer: Replace the feed-forward block with N expert FFNs and a learned router. The router scores every token against all N experts and dispatches it to the top-k, usually k=2. Compute scales with k, not N, so parameter count and FLOPs decouple. The cost moves from compute to memory and to balance: every expert must be resident, and a router that favours a few experts wastes the rest while overflowing its favourites past their capacity factor.
bodies.math: For token x, the router computes g = softmax(W_r · x) over N experts and selects T = top-k(g). The output is y = Σ_{i∈T} (g_i / Σ_{j∈T} g_j) · E_i(x), so the mixture stays a convex combination of the chosen experts. Training adds an auxiliary load-balancing loss, typically α · N · Σ_i f_i · P_i, where f_i is the fraction of tokens routed to expert i and P_i the mean router probability for it. The product is minimised when both are uniform.
